analysis.one_liner: Directs the FTC to study drug supply-chain middlemen and recommend fixes for anticompetitive drug pricing.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Senate committee sent the bill to the Senate floor calendar in March 2023, but it never came up for a vote before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would order the Federal Trade Commission to investigate pharmacy benefit managers — the middlemen that decide which drugs your insurance covers and what pharmacies get paid — and report within a year on whether they charge employers more than they pay pharmacies, steer patients to pharmacies they own, use patients' data against competitors, or favor pricier drugs on their lists. It would also require an interim report in 180 days and a report on complaints about sole-source drug manufacturers, with recommendations for laws that make drug pricing more competitive. It creates no new rules itself; it builds the record Congress would need to act.
analysis.who_benefits: People who fill prescriptions and employers and insurers that pay for them, by creating an official government record of how pharmacy benefit managers operate — the first step toward rules or enforcement that could lower drug costs. Community pharmacies that compete against pharmacies owned by the same middlemen would also gain a documented case for fairer treatment.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Prescription drug buyers and local pharmacies

how_it_helps.text: Requires the FTC to report within one year — with an interim report in 180 days — on whether pharmacy benefit managers charge payers more than they reimburse pharmacies, steer patients to pharmacies they own, use competitor pharmacies' proprietary data for their own advantage, and use formulary design to push higher-cost drugs [S4].

Requires the FTC to recommend policies to improve transparency and competition in the pharmaceutical supply chain, prevent anticompetitive behavior, and make sure consumers capture savings from mergers [S4].
Also requires a report on anticompetitive conduct by sole-source drug manufacturers and on legal obstacles that keep the FTC from enforcing antitrust law in the drug supply chain [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Pharmacy benefit managers and their parent companies, which would face an official investigation into their pricing and business practices and could see subsequent legislation or enforcement limit their revenue. The direct cost of the bill itself is small — a government study.
analysis.who_pays_short: Pharmacy benefit managers and their owners

drawbacks.text: The bill does not itself lower anyone's drug bill. It only orders a study and recommendations; actual relief would require further legislation the bill does not contain [S4].

It leaves the FTC's conclusions a year away from enactment and provides no deadline for Congress to act on the recommendations, so a study could become a substitute for action rather than a step toward it [S4].
Critics of study-only measures would note the FTC already has authority to investigate and sue over anticompetitive conduct; the bill adds reporting duties rather than new enforcement power [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct cost is minor and the potential benefit — a government record of how drug middlemen operate, with recommendations for fixing it — is a reasonable first step on a problem that affects nearly everyone who takes prescription medicine. But the bill's honest weakness is that it defers: no prices fall because of it, and a study can be a way to appear to act. It was designed as groundwork, not relief, and even as groundwork it never reached a vote.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Judiciary Committee approved it unanimously-style with bipartisan support and put it on the Senate's calendar of business, but Senate leadership never brought it up for a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Chuck Grassley introduced the bill on January 26, 2023, and it was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee [S1,S6].
It had 21 cosponsors split evenly across parties: 10 of 48 Senate Democrats, 10 of 49 Senate Republicans, and 1 of 4 Independents [S5].

The Judiciary Committee ordered it reported favorably with a substitute amendment on February 9, 2023, and reported it on March 1, 2023, placing it on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 19) [S6].
The bill was never scheduled for a Senate floor vote, never passed either chamber, and died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmacy benefit managers and their parent companies came out ahead: no FTC report on their practices was ever mandated, and no follow-up legislation got a building block. The bill's bipartisan cosponsors got no result, and prescription drug buyers got no new information or protection from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Pharmacy benefit managers, and the record stays closed

for.name: Chuck Grassley
for.role: U.S. Senator (R-IA), bill sponsor and Judiciary Committee ranking member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gathered bipartisan cosponsors; his committee reported it to the Senate floor calendar.

for.name: Dick Durbin
for.what_they_did: Reported the bill out of committee favorably with a substitute amendment on March 1, 2023, placing it on the Senate Legislative Calendar.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship split evenly across parties — 10 Democrats, 10 Republicans, and 1 Independent — and the Democratic committee chair reported it out favorably; no senator is recorded as opposing it, and the bill died from never being scheduled, not from a party fight.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers (CVS Caremark, Express Scripts, Optum Rx and their parent companies)
industries.note: The bill would put these companies under an official FTC examination of spread pricing, patient steering to their own pharmacies, use of competitors' data, and formulary design that favors costlier drugs — practices that pad their revenue at the expense of employers, insurers, and patients. A mandated report is the standard first step toward regulation or enforcement that would shrink those profits.

The FTC study would document practices — including reimbursement rates that favor pharmacies the middlemen own — that community pharmacies say drive them out of business; a documented record could support fairer treatment for them. Local pharmacies disappearing narrows where people can fill prescriptions affordably.

The bill also requires a report on complaints of anticompetitive conduct by sole-source drug makers and the FTC's ability to act on them, which could lead to enforcement against manufacturers of drugs without generic equivalents. Sole-source makers lose exposure; makers of lower-cost competing drugs could gain if formulary practices that favor higher-cost drugs come under scrutiny.
